title: How to keep reading
hook: a few lines a day, one line carried: the way to read any old book

segments.voice: Yesterday, the emperor and the mystic, a thousand years apart. Your line was they don't merge. Did you catch two voices being blended? Day two hundred twenty-nine.

There's a kind of book that ends up on a nightstand. A big old one, bought in a burst of good intention, read for three nights, then used as a coaster. Maybe the problem isn't the book, or the reader. Maybe it's the method. Old books get read the way the news gets read: fast, for information, all at once. They were never written for that. For seventy-odd days this camp has read two old books a few lines at a time. Today, how to keep reading.
screen: `THE BOOK ON THE NIGHTSTAND.` → `READ LIKE THE NEWS.` → `HOW TO KEEP READING.`

segments.voice: The Roman writer Seneca, a Stoic who wrote long before Marcus, gives this advice in his second letter to his friend Lucilius. Don't wander through piles of authors, he says. Stay with a few great ones and digest them. Food that comes straight back up doesn't nourish anyone. In Richard Gummere's 1917 translation, he puts it in three words: "Everywhere means nowhere." Then Seneca describes his own habit. Each day, out of everything he reads, he picks one thought to chew on for the rest of the day. And in that very letter he does it, picking a line from another philosopher, Epicurus, about poverty that's content being an honorable thing. One thought, carried. Christian monks worked out something similar. A medieval Carthusian monk named Guigo described a ladder of four steps for reading scripture slowly: reading, then turning the words over, then prayer, then resting in silence. It's called lectio divina, holy reading, and it is still practiced today. Different aims, different sources, the same rhythm: slow, little, and kept. So here's the method for any old book, sacred or not. Three lines a day. Read them slowly, twice. Pick one phrase. Carry it until evening. That's all. Three lines a day is more than a thousand lines a year. The Meditations, the Masnavi, the Psalms, the Gita, the Dhammapada: none of them has to be finished on a weekend.
screen: `EVERYWHERE MEANS NOWHERE.` · `ONE THOUGHT, CHEWED ALL DAY.` · `LECTIO DIVINA: FOUR SLOW STEPS.` · `READ SLOWLY, PICK ONE, CARRY IT.` · then, large: `THREE LINES A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read three lines slowly. If there's a book nearby, open it anywhere and take three lines. If not, use three lines you know by heart. Settle and breathe. Read or say the first line, word by word, as if each word cost money. Then the second. Then the third. Now go back, and let one phrase rise. Hold just that phrase for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
How to keep reading. A few lines a day, read slowly, one phrase carried: Seneca's habit, and the monks' holy reading. Today's word.
Your line: three lines a day. Today, choose the old book you'll keep reading after this camp, and put it where your phone usually sits at night. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Some readers of old texts read a few lines a day and carry one phrase, as Seneca describes in his second letter; Christians who keep lectio divina read scripture in the same slow way.

what a scholar hears: Seneca, Letter 2, where he quotes Epicurus; Guigo II's Ladder of Monks names the four steps: lectio, meditatio, oratio, contemplatio.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook no longer tells the listener about their nightstand or says 'it worked'; cut 'a century before', 'twelfth century', 'many Christians' and the unsourced 'read this way for centuries' claim; replaced the unsourced myth item with Seneca's own habit.
